pregunta: How does fine-tuning compare with retrieval-augmented generation for answering questions about our company’s policies and products?
respuesta: Fine-tuning teaches a model how to respond—such as using your company’s tone or following a specific workflow—but it is not the best way to keep policy and product facts current. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) searches approved company documents at question time and uses them to answer, making updates easier and answers easier to verify. For questions like “What is our return policy?”, RAG is usually the better choice. Fine-tuning can complement it when you also need consistent language or task behavior.
respuesta_estudiante: Fine-tuning is a way to test the accuracy of answers against actual responses—for example, asking whether a policy will be enforced by law or not; then retraining it on new examples that match those rules. Retrieval-augmented generation can answer more complex queries but may require human review before use. For instance, ask whether a product has been tested at least 10 times (retrained) versus only once: “Is this version accurate?” Fine-tune might help identify errors while still allow users to choose what they want without needing approval from human reviewers.
comentario: La respuesta confunde el ajuste fino con la evaluación de exactitud y no explica que RAG consulta documentos actualizados para responder preguntas sobre políticas y productos.

pregunta: What are common prompt-writing mistakes that lead to vague, inaccurate, or overly confident answers?
respuesta: Common mistakes include giving a vague task (“analyze our performance”) without defining the goal, audience, or success criteria; omitting key context such as market, time period, or source data; combining too many requests; using ambiguous terms; and failing to specify the desired format. Asking for current facts without providing sources can invite fabricated details. Leading questions, or demanding certainty when evidence is limited, can produce biased or overconfident answers. State assumptions, request evidence, and ask the model to flag uncertainty.
respuesta_estudiante: Common mistake: Using a question as the sole basis for a response without checking its accuracy; using it only when asked—not enough context is needed; providing too much detail but not sufficient information; failing to test assumptions before testing results; including irrelevant details unless they’re relevant; asking questions with unclear definitions; giving responses based on hearsay or personal opinions rather than facts; overusing language like “it will work” instead of explaining what works well.
comentario: Menciona la falta de contexto, las definiciones ambiguas y el exceso de confianza, pero incluye frases confusas y omite errores clave como no especificar el formato, combinar demasiadas tareas o pedir datos actuales sin fuentes.

pregunta: How do we measure whether a RAG system is retrieving the right information and giving reliable answers, rather than just sounding convincing?
respuesta: Build a test set of real business questions with verified answers and source documents. Measure retrieval precision and recall: did the system find the right evidence, without burying it in irrelevant results? Score answer correctness, factual support by retrieved sources, and citation accuracy separately. Test whether it abstains when evidence is missing or conflicting. Have domain experts review edge cases, then monitor these measures and user-reported errors in production. Track task outcomes, not fluency: a polished answer without verifiable evidence is a failure.
respuesta_estudiante: Use metrics such as accuracy (the percentage of relevant data retrieved), relevance—whether it’s useful for what you need to answer, consistency across sources, and human review)—and reliability: check that retrieval times match expected usage; don’t rely on vague or unsupported claims; test against real-world examples; and verify results by crosschecking them with other sources before sharing. For example, use a model trained on news articles instead of headlines when evaluating its credibility.
comentario: Incluye pruebas con ejemplos reales y revisión humana, pero confunde la precisión de recuperación con la exactitud, omite evaluar por separado las respuestas y sus citas, y añade criterios irrelevantes como los tiempos de recuperación y el ejemplo de noticias.

pregunta: Can an AI agent reliably handle supplier invoices and purchase approvals, or should a human review every decision?
respuesta: An AI agent can reliably automate routine checks—such as matching invoices to purchase orders, validating amounts and flagging missing information—if it uses approved systems, clear rules and audit logs. A human need not review every low-risk match. Escalate exceptions, high-value purchases, new suppliers, bank-detail changes and policy overrides for human approval. Keep approval limits and separation of duties in place, and regularly sample decisions to catch errors or drift.
respuesta_estudiante: An agent can process invoice receipts but cannot verify the accuracy of sales data; approve purchases only when approved by authorized parties—typically customers who have valid contracts with the vendor. Human reviewers check compliance, such as payment terms, delivery dates, and return policies. For example, a retailer might require approval for orders from a trusted source before approving them to prevent errors during shipping.
comentario: La respuesta menciona controles humanos, pero confunde las aprobaciones de compras con autorizaciones de clientes y no explica qué verificaciones rutinarias puede automatizar la IA ni cuándo escalar excepciones.

pregunta: Can an LLM understand a customer’s intent, or is it mainly matching patterns in language? What does that distinction mean for a bank in Chile?
respuesta: An LLM can often infer a customer’s likely intent from context, but it does so through learned language patterns—not human understanding. It can misread Chilean expressions, ambiguous requests, or unusual cases. For a Chilean bank, this makes it useful for routing queries, summarizing requests, or drafting answers, but risky as the sole decision-maker for credit, fraud, or complaints. Use local testing, privacy safeguards, clear escalation to staff, and human review for consequential decisions.
respuesta_estudiante: An LLM can recognize the context of what customers say—whether they need help with something like checking account balances or making payments; whether their answer matches what someone else might ask (e.g., “Do you have any questions?”); how often they will hear from them; when they may be asked again; whereabouts during each conversation; and who has access to those conversations. It doesn't necessarily know why people do things differently: For example, a customer might use a different credit card than another person because one isn’t available at home but works out well on the go. pregunta: When should we use a prompt template instead of writing a new prompt for every task?
respuesta: Use a prompt template when tasks recur with a consistent goal and structure, but the inputs change—for example, drafting customer-service replies or summarizing invoices. Templates improve consistency, save time, and make it easier to test and govern outputs across teams. Write a new prompt when the task is one-off, exploratory, or requires substantially different context or reasoning.
respuesta_estudiante: Use prompts when you need to ask the same question repeatedly or have multiple related tasks; write it once with clear instructions—for example, “Write this report.” For each task, choose one prompt that covers all possible cases: include examples, clarify requirements, track progress, set deadlines, test assumptions, and check results. Then edit only those parts where they fail. Use templates whenever you can’t find a single-purpose prompt; save your best work as a draft before moving on to another task.
comentario: Reconoce que una plantilla sirve para tareas repetidas o relacionadas, pero añade recomendaciones irrelevantes y aconseja usarla de forma demasiado general, sin distinguir las tareas puntuales o que requieren un enfoque distinto.

pregunta: How could our customer service team use prompts to draft helpful responses in Chilean Spanish without sounding generic?
respuesta: Give the model the customer’s issue, relevant account history, product details, and the outcome you can offer. Specify a warm, clear Chilean Spanish tone, your brand voice, and any required policies; ask it to avoid generic apologies and forced slang. For example: “Draft a concise reply that acknowledges [specific issue], explains [next step] and uses natural Chilean Spanish. Don’t invent facts; ask for missing information.” Have agents verify details before sending.
respuesta_estudiante: Use a prompt that asks the user what they need help with—for example: “¿Cuál es la pregunta?” (What is it?) or “¡Qué puede hacer esta información?” This helps users understand their task rather than asking for general advice. For instance, instead of saying “help me find my car,” ask how you can get there; then provide examples like finding a parking spot at a nearby store or getting directions from a friend’s address. Use simple language and avoid using phrases like “do this” when someone already knows something

pregunta: What infrastructure and ongoing costs should we expect if we deploy RAG for a few hundred employees across our Chilean operations?
respuesta: For a few hundred employees, a cloud-based RAG pilot might cost roughly US$1,000–5,000/month; a production service with higher usage, stronger availability and support may be US$5,000–20,000+/month. Main costs: model/API usage, cloud compute, document storage and indexing, vector search, monitoring, backups, security and egress. Usage and document volume drive costs more than headcount. Budget separately for initial integration, data cleanup and ongoing administration. For Chile, check regional hosting, latency, data-residency requirements and cross-border transfer costs before choosing a provider.

  • A backup plan includes two copies (one on local servers and one at remote locations) that contain only critical data while protecting backups from loss during emergencies.

pregunta: What kinds of business data are useful for fine-tuning, and how much high-quality data would a company typically need?
respuesta: Useful fine-tuning data consists of high-quality examples of the behavior you want: customer-service questions and approved replies, document-to-field extraction, request classification, or sales emails in the company’s preferred style. Use representative, accurate, consistently formatted data, with sensitive information removed and usage rights confirmed—not simply a dump of company documents. A narrow task may benefit from a few hundred examples; many projects start with 500–2,000, while broader or more varied tasks may need several thousand. Validate performance on separate examples; quality and coverage matter more than volume.

For most businesses:

  • Sales targets should include customer demographics, purchase history, and billing statuses.
  • Financial statements may require detailed financial records but not too many examples.

pregunta: What is the difference between an LLM’s training data and the information it can access through a company’s internal documents?
respuesta: Training data is the material used to teach an LLM patterns and knowledge before deployment. Company documents are separate information the model may retrieve at response time through connected tools, such as search or retrieval-augmented generation. They can provide private, current context without changing the model’s training. Access depends on permissions and system configuration; the model cannot see internal documents unless they are explicitly connected and made available.
respuesta_estudiante: An LLM uses trained examples to generate responses; its knowledge may not be available for use by other sources or when asked questions that require human judgment—such as legal advice or customer service instructions. It also has limited control over how it interacts with external materials (e.g., emails), so it cannot answer complex queries without explicit approval from a source. For example, a retailer might ask an employee about a product recommendation but only have access to approved sales records.
comentario: Menciona que el modelo aprende de ejemplos, pero confunde esa formación con el acceso a documentos internos y añade afirmaciones imprecisas, sin explicar que estos pueden consultarse mediante herramientas conectadas sin modificar el entrenamiento.

pregunta: What is an AI agent, and how is it different from a chatbot that only answers questions?
respuesta: An AI agent is a system that can pursue a goal by planning steps, using tools or company systems, and adjusting based on results. A chatbot that only answers questions responds with information but does not take action. For example, a chatbot can explain an invoice policy; an agent could check an invoice against that policy, flag discrepancies, and create a task for the finance team—subject to permissions and human oversight.
respuesta_estudiante: An AI agent is trained to perform specific tasks or make decisions based on input data; its responses may not always match what the user asks for—for example, asking “what’s wrong with this?” instead of explaining why something isn’t working. An AI can answer facts but lacks human judgment: It doesn’t know when a question has no relevant context or if someone might misinterpret it. For instance, a customer service agent would ask about a product issue without knowing whether customers have purchased it before. pregunta: When should a company use a single AI agent rather than a team of agents with different roles?
respuesta: Use a single AI agent when the task is well-defined, follows a mostly linear workflow, and needs the same context and tools throughout. For example, one agent can review supplier invoices, check them against policy, and draft an exception report. A single agent is usually simpler, faster, cheaper, and easier to monitor. Use a team of agents when work benefits from distinct expertise, parallel analysis, or independent checks—such as combining legal, financial, and market assessments.
respuesta_estudiante: Use a single agent when: It can handle high-value tasks quickly; it has limited access to sensitive information or data; the task is complex enough that multiple agents will work together without overlapping responsibilities; you need only one person for each role—not too few but not too many either (one per department). For example, a customer service agent might be responsible for handling sales requests while also answering questions about product reviews.
comentario: La respuesta confunde cuándo conviene un solo agente con escenarios de varios agentes y no menciona los criterios clave: tarea bien definida, flujo lineal y contexto y herramientas constantes.
